reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: A multisystem disorder characterised by benign hamartomas in the brain, skin, heart, kidneys, lungs and eyes, following autosomal dominant inheritance with a high de novo rate
Skin findings are key diagnostic clues: hypomelanotic macules (best seen under Wood's lamp), facial angiofibromas, shagreen patches and periungual fibromas
Neurological features include cortical tubers, subependymal nodules and subependymal giant cell astrocytomas, with epilepsy (often infantile spasms) and TSC-associated neuropsychiatric disorders
Cardiac rhabdomyomas may be detected antenatally or in infancy and usually regress spontaneously
Renal angiomyolipomas and cysts require surveillance because of the risk of haemorrhage and, rarely, malignancy, and are a leading cause of adult morbidity
Lymphangioleiomyomatosis, causing progressive cystic lung disease, predominantly affects women and warrants respiratory monitoring
The mTOR pathway is constitutively activated, and mTOR inhibitors are an established targeted therapy for several manifestations
reference.pathophysiology: Tuberous sclerosis complex is caused by loss-of-function variants in TSC1 (encoding hamartin) or TSC2 (encoding tuberin), whose protein product forms a complex that inhibits the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signalling pathway. Loss of this inhibitory brake leads to constitutive mTOR activation, driving unregulated cell growth and proliferation and the formation of hamartomas in multiple organs. A second-hit somatic inactivation of the remaining allele in individual cells underlies lesion development, and TSC2 variants generally produce a more severe phenotype than TSC1.
additionalDifferentials: Multiple endocrine neoplasia and other hamartoma syndromes
Isolated infantile spasms of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis of TSC1 and TSC2
Brain MRI for tubers, subependymal nodules and giant cell astrocytoma, with electroencephalography for seizures
Renal imaging (ultrasound or MRI) for angiomyolipomas and cysts with periodic surveillance
Echocardiography and electrocardiography for rhabdomyomas and arrhythmia
Pulmonary function testing and chest imaging for lymphangioleiomyomatosis in at-risk individuals
redFlags: New or worsening headache, vomiting or focal deficit suggesting an enlarging subependymal giant cell astrocytoma with hydrocephalus
Flank pain, haematuria or shock from angiomyolipoma haemorrhage
Progressive breathlessness or pneumothorax from lymphangioleiomyomatosis
Infantile spasms requiring prompt recognition and treatment
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is highly variable and depends on the burden of neurological, renal and pulmonary disease; epilepsy and neuropsychiatric disorders drive childhood morbidity, while renal and pulmonary complications dominate in adults. Targeted mTOR-inhibitor therapy and structured surveillance have improved outcomes, and many individuals live into adulthood.
pitfalls: Overlooking subtle hypomelanotic macules without Wood's-lamp examination
Failing to establish lifelong renal surveillance for angiomyolipoma growth and bleeding risk
Missing an enlarging subependymal giant cell astrocytoma causing obstructive hydrocephalus
Not recognising TSC-associated neuropsychiatric disorders, which are frequently under-assessed and undertreated
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
International Tuberous Sclerosis Complex Consensus Group recommendations
management: Everolimus or another mTOR inhibitor as disease-modifying therapy for subependymal giant cell astrocytomas, enlarging renal angiomyolipomas and lymphangioleiomyomatosis
Epilepsy control with antiseizure medication, using vigabatrin as first-line for infantile spasms and considering epilepsy surgery or vagus nerve stimulation in drug-resistant seizures
Topical mTOR inhibitor (sirolimus) or laser therapy for facial angiofibromas, with screening and support for TSC-associated neuropsychiatric disorders
Structured surveillance with serial brain MRI, renal imaging, echocardiography and pulmonary function testing for the multisystem complications
Manage acute angiomyolipoma haemorrhage with selective arterial embolisation and nephron-sparing measures rather than nephrectomy where possible
Multidisciplinary care across neurology, nephrology, dermatology, respiratory and ophthalmology
Genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal dominant inheritance and the high de novo rate
